statement: Let \(K\) be a field of characteristic \(0\), let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(\mathbb Z\)-graded \(K\)-vector space with \(V^n=0\) for \(n<0\) and \(n>2d\), let \(L:V\to V\) be \(K\)-linear with \(L(V^n)\subseteq V^{n+2}\) such that \(L^{\,d-n}:V^n\to V^{2d-n}\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\), and put \(P^r=\ker\bigl(L^{\,d-r+1}:V^r\to V^{2d-r+2}\bigr)\), with \(P^m=0\) for \(m<0\) and for \(m>d\). Let \(F:V\to V\) be a \(K\)-linear automorphism commuting with \(L\) and preserving each \(V^n\). Then for every \(0\le r\le d\) the characteristic polynomial of \(F|_{V^r}\) in \(K[t]\) equals \(\prod_{k\ge0}\chi(F|_{P^{r-2k}})\), the characteristic polynomials of the \(F|_{P^{r-2k}}\).
proof:
We write the grading as V_n := V^n to match the notation of the cited lemma Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_523; this is only a change of notation.

STEP 0 (Setup). K has characteristic 0, V = \oplus_{n\in\mathbb Z} V_n is finite dimensional with V_n = 0 for n<0 and n>2d, L\in\mathrm{End}_K(V) with L(V_n)\subseteq V_{n+2}, and L^{d-n}:V_n\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2d-n} is an isomorphism for 0\le n\le d. For 0\le m\le d, P^m := \ker(L^{d-m+1}:V_m\to V_{2d-m+2}), and P^m:=0 for m<0 and for m>d. F\in\mathrm{GL}_K(V) with F\circ L = L\circ F and F(V_n)\subseteq V_n for all n.

STEP 1 (F^{-1} also commutes with L and preserves the grading).
(a) Commutation: from FL = LF, left-multiplying by F^{-1} gives L = F^{-1}LF; right-multiplying this last equality by F^{-1} gives LF^{-1} = F^{-1}L, i.e. F^{-1}L = LF^{-1}.
(b) Grading: for each n, F(V_n)\subseteq V_n and F is injective, so F|_{V_n}:V_n\to V_n is injective, hence bijective since V_n is finite dimensional; thus F(V_n)=V_n. If y\in V_n, write y = Fx with x\in V_n; then F^{-1}y = x\in V_n, so F^{-1}(V_n)\subseteq V_n.

STEP 2 (Each P^m is F-stable and F^{-1}-stable; F|_{P^m} is an automorphism of P^m).
For m<0 or m>d we have P^m=0, so there is nothing to prove. Let 0\le m\le d. Take x\in P^m; then x\in V_m and L^{d-m+1}x=0. Since F preserves the grading, Fx\in V_m, and by Step 1(a) applied d-m+1 times, L^{d-m+1}(Fx) = F(L^{d-m+1}x) = F(0) = 0. Hence Fx\in P^m, so F(P^m)\subseteq P^m. The identical argument with F replaced by F^{-1} (valid by Step 1) gives F^{-1}(P^m)\subseteq P^m. These two inclusions yield F(P^m)=P^m, so F restricts to an automorphism F|_{P^m}\in\mathrm{GL}_K(P^m); in particular its characteristic polynomial \chi(F|_{P^m})\in K[t] is defined. (For m<0 or m>d, F|_{P^m} is the identity on the zero space and \chi(F|_{P^m})=1.)

STEP 3 (The primitive decomposition in degrees 0\le r\le d is F-equivariant).
Fix r with 0\le r\le d. Consider
  \Phi_r : \bigoplus_{k\ge 0} P^{r-2k} \longrightarrow V_r, \qquad (x_k)_k \longmapsto \sum_{k\ge 0} L^{k}x_k .
This is well defined: for k > r/2 one has r-2k<0, hence P^{r-2k}=0 by convention, so only the finitely many k with 0\le k\le\lfloor r/2\rfloor contribute; and for x_k\in P^{r-2k}\subseteq V_{r-2k}, L^k x_k\in V_{r-2k+2k}=V_r, so the sum lands in V_r.

We now apply Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_523 to the data (K,d,V_\bullet,L). Its hypotheses are exactly those of Step 0 (K has characteristic 0, V is finite dimensional, V_n=0 for n<0 and n>2d, L(V_n)\subseteq V_{n+2}, and L^{d-n}:V_n\xrightarrow{\sim}V_{2d-n} for 0\le n\le d), and its definition of P^r coincides with ours, including the conventions P^m=0 for m<0 and m>d. The lemma asserts that for every n with 0\le n\le 2d the addition map \bigoplus_{k\ge\max(0,n-d)} P^{n-2k}\to V_n, (x_k)\mapsto\sum_k L^k x_k, is a K-linear isomorphism. We apply it ONLY in degrees n=r with 0\le r\le d. In that range \max(0,r-d)=0, so the index set of the direct sum is exactly \{k\ge 0\}, and therefore \Phi_r is an isomorphism
  \bigoplus_{k\ge 0} P^{r-2k} \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } V_r . \qquad (\ast)
(We deliberately do not use the lemma for n>d, where the lower bound \max(0,n-d) is strictly positive and the unrestricted sum over all k\ge 0 would not map isomorphically.)

Let \Psi_r := \bigoplus_{k\ge 0} F|_{P^{r-2k}} be the automorphism of \oplus_{k\ge0}P^{r-2k} acting componentwise; it is well defined by Step 2. For (x_k)_k in the direct sum,
  \Phi_r(\Psi_r((x_k)_k)) = \Phi_r((Fx_k)_k) = \sum_{k\ge0} L^k(Fx_k) = \sum_{k\ge0} F(L^k x_k) = F\Big(\sum_{k\ge0} L^k x_k\Big) = F(\Phi_r((x_k)_k)),
where the middle equality uses Step 1(a) applied k times, and the exchange of F with the finite sum uses K-linearity of F. Thus
  \Phi_r\circ\Psi_r = F|_{V_r}\circ\Phi_r ,
and since \Phi_r is invertible by (\ast),
  F|_{V_r} = \Phi_r\circ\Psi_r\circ\Phi_r^{-1}. \qquad (\ast\ast)

STEP 4 (Conjugate operators have the same characteristic polynomial). Choose a K-basis B of V_r; then Mat(F|_{V_r},B) and Mat(\Psi_r,\Phi_r^{-1}B) represent the same operator under two bases, since (\ast\ast) says precisely that \Phi_r is a change-of-basis identification between (\oplus_k P^{r-2k},\Psi_r) and (V_r,F|_{V_r}). Hence their characteristic polynomials agree: \chi(F|_{V_r}) = \chi(\Psi_r).

STEP 5 (Characteristic polynomial of a direct sum is the product). Put k_0:=\lfloor r/2\rfloor; the only possibly nonzero summands of \oplus_{k\ge0}P^{r-2k} are P^{r},P^{r-2},\dots,P^{r-2k_0}. For each 0\le k\le k_0 choose a basis B_k of P^{r-2k} (the empty basis if P^{r-2k}=0), and let B = \bigsqcup_k B_k, a basis of the direct sum. The matrix A of \Psi_r in B is block diagonal: A = \mathrm{diag}(A_0,A_1,\dots,A_{k_0}) with A_k = Mat(F|_{P^{r-2k}},B_k). Indeed \Psi_r preserves each summand, so for i in the index set I_k of B_k and j in I_{k'} with k\neq k' the (i,j)-entry of A is 0. Then tI-A is likewise block diagonal, \mathrm{diag}(tI-A_0,\dots,tI-A_{k_0}). Expanding the determinant by permutations: writing the index set as the disjoint union \bigsqcup_k I_k, the entry (tI-A)_{i,j} vanishes whenever i\in I_k,\ j\in I_{k'} with k\neq k'; hence a permutation \sigma contributing a nonzero term \mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i (tI-A)_{i,\sigma(i)} must satisfy \sigma(I_k)=I_k for every k, and the sum over such \sigma factors as the product of the sums over the \sigma|_{I_k}. Thus \det(tI-A)=\prod_{k=0}^{k_0}\det(tI-A_k), i.e.
  \chi(\Psi_r) = \prod_{k=0}^{k_0}\chi(F|_{P^{r-2k}}).
For k>k_0 the space P^{r-2k} is the zero space and \chi(F|_{P^{r-2k}})=1, so appending those factors does not change the product:
  \chi(\Psi_r) = \prod_{k\ge0}\chi(F|_{P^{r-2k}}).

STEP 6 (Conclusion). Combining Steps 4 and 5,
  \chi(F|_{V^r}) = \chi(F|_{V_r}) = \chi(\Psi_r) = \prod_{k\ge0}\chi(F|_{P^{r-2k}}),
which is the required identity for every 0\le r\le d.

STEP 7 (Edge cases). If d=0 then r=0 is the only case: V=V_0, P^0=\ker(L:V_0\to V_2)=V_0 since V_2=0, and the product reduces to the single factor k=0 (all other factors are 1 because r-2k<0), giving the tautology \chi(F|_{V^0})=\chi(F|_{P^0}); the argument above covers it. If r=0 the same holds. If P^{r-2k}=0 for some k, the corresponding factor is 1 by the convention P^m=0, consistently with Step 5. All cases are thus covered, and the proof is complete.
